query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled fraction of silicon carbide (SiC) as a reactive additive into the ZrB2 precursor can enable liquid‐phase assisted sintering at lower temperatures (~1700–1800 °C) while producing an in‐situ protective SiO2 phase at the grain boundaries that improves mechanical integrity, oxidation durability, and resistance to liquid metal plating corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 powders that require sintering above 2300 °C for full densification but show vulnerabilities when processed at lower temperatures.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small, optimized amount (e.g., 5–10 wt%) of SiC into the ZrB2 precursor mix and use a reactive, liquid-phase assisted sintering method under controlled atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Sintering performed at reduced temperatures (around 1700–1800 °C) under an atmosphere that permits transient liquid formation and partial oxidation of SiC; designed for high-temperature service, including exposure to oxidative and liquid metal plating environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an intergranular, nanoscale SiO2 phase (from partial oxidation of SiC) at the grain boundaries of the ZrB2 matrix.
generation.mechanism: SiC addition lowers the sintering temperature by generating a transient liquid phase that enhances densification and bonding. During high-temperature service, the SiC-derived SiO2 phase forms a continuous protective network that impedes oxygen penetration and limits metal ion diffusion, thereby reducing oxidation rates and mitigating liquid metal-induced corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The SiC-modified ZrB2 composite will achieve high density and adequate mechanical strength at sintering temperatures near 1800 °C while exhibiting markedly improved oxidation resistance and liquid metal plating corrosion resistance compared with pure high-temperature sintered ZrB2 and previously reported low-temperature processed specimens.
generation.baseline: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 processed at >2300 °C, which shows excellent intrinsic bonding but is difficult and energy-intensive to manufacture; earlier low-temperature approaches yielded materials vulnerable to oxidation and corrosion.
generation.boundary: This strategy is expected to be effective when sintering temperatures are maintained between 1700–1800 °C and under service conditions where the in-situ formed SiO2 phase remains stable; outcomes may be sensitive to the precise SiC content and processing atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal SiC concentration and precise processing parameters required to consistently form the protective SiO2 phase are not yet determined. Additionally, the long-term stability of the intergranular SiO2 layer under varied service conditions introduces some uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) a baseline set of pure ZrB2 sintered at >2300 °C, and (2) a test set of ZrB2 with 5–10 wt% SiC sintered via reactive liquid-phase assisted sintering at ~1800 °C. Perform microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS, TEM) to assess densification and the formation of intergranular SiO2. Then, subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests and liquid metal plating corrosion tests.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size, phase distribution via SEM/EDS and TEM)
High-temperature oxidation testing (measuring weight gain/loss, oxide layer thickness)
Liquid metal plating corrosion tests (corrosion rate measurements, surface analysis post-exposure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SiC-modified ZrB2 specimens do not demonstrate a significant reduction in sintering temperature, fail to develop a continuous and protective SiO2 intergranular phase, or do not exhibit improved oxidation and corrosion resistance compared to both the conventional high-temperature sintered ZrB2 and prior low-temperature processed materials, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Synthesis and Characterization of High-Purity, High-Entropy Diboride Ceramic Powders by a Liquid Phase Method

Abstract: AbstractA nano-dual-phase powder with ultra-fine grain size was synthesized by the liquid precursor method at 1200 °C. A series of single-phase high-entropy ceramic powders ((Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2) with high purity (C content less than 0.9 wt% and O content less than 0.7 wt%) and ultrafine (average grain sizes of 340–570 nm) were successfully synthesized at 1800 °C. The sample of (TiZrHfNbTa)B2 exhibited a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, and the metal elements were uniformly distributed at the nanoscale, microscale, and macroscale. This method did not apply to the preparation of all high-entropy ceramic powders and was unfavorable for the formation of single-phase high-entropy borides when the size difference factor exceeded 3.9%. The present work provides a guide for the development of ceramic-based composites through precursor impregnation pyrolysis.Keywords: liquid-phase precursor method, high-entropy diboride powders, solid solutions, microstructure, pyrolysis mechanism

High-Entropy Diborides—Silicon Carbide Composites by Reactive and Non-Reactive Spark Plasma Sintering: A Comparative Study

Abstract: AbstractThe reactive spark plasma sintering (R-SPS) method was compared in this work with the two-step SHS–SPS route, based on the combination of the self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) with the SPS process, for the fabrication of dense (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2)B2–SiC and (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2Ta0.2Zr0.2)B2–SiC ceramics. A multiphase and inhomogeneous product, containing various borides, was obtained at 2000 °C/20 min by R-SPS from transition metals, B4C, and Si. In contrast, if the same precursors were first reacted by SHS and then processed by SPS under the optimized condition of 1800 °C/20 min, the desired ceramics were successfully attained. The resulting sintered samples possessed relative densities above 97% and displayed uniform microstructures with residual oxide content <2.4 wt.%. The presence of SiC made the sintering temperature milder, i.e., 150 °C below that needed by the corresponding additive-free system. Rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering of high-entropy ceramic composites

Abstract: High-entropy ceramics and their composites display high mechanical strength and attractive high-temperature stabilities. However, properties like strong covalent bond character and low self-diffusion coefficients make them difficult to get sintered, limiting their mass popularity. Here, we present a rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering strategy and use high-entropy metal diboride/boron carbide composite as a proof of concept. We use a carbon-based heater to fast-heat the composite to around 3000 K, and a small fraction of eutectic liquid was formed at the interface between high-entropy metal diborides and boron carbide. A crystalline dodecaboride intergranular phase was generated upon cooling to ameliorate the adhesion between the components. The as-sintered composite presents a high hardness of 36.4 GPa at a load of 0.49 N and 24.4 GPa at a load of 9.8 N. This liquid phase–assisted rapid ultrahigh-temperature strategy can be widely applicable for other ultrahigh-temperature ceramics as well.
